{{Short description|American-born Canadian chemist (1934–2018)}}
'''Cooper Harold Langford III''' {{post-nominals|country=CAN|FRSC}} (October 14, 1934 – March 11, 2018) was an American-born Canadian chemist.

==Biography==
He was born to the philosopher [[Cooper Harold Langford]] and his first wife, Susan Coffman, in [[Ann Arbor, Michigan]] on October 14, 1934. He attended [[Harvard University]] as an undergraduate, and [[Northwestern University]] for graduate studies. His work at Northwestern and his postgraduate work at [[University College London]] and [[Columbia University]] resulted in the publication (with [[Harry B. Gray]]) of [[Ligand]] Substitution Processes (1966).<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechBOOK:1966.001|title=Ligand Substitution Processes|first1=Cooper H.|last1=Langford|first2=Harry B.|last2=Gray|date=March 10, 1966|publisher=W. A. Benjamin, Inc.|via=authors.library.caltech.edu}}</ref> The Langford-Gray classification remains an important tool to describe the mechanics of inorganic chemical reactions.

Langford taught at [[Amherst College]] in [[Amherst, Massachusetts]], [[Carleton University]] in [[Ottawa, Canada]], [[Concordia University]] in [[Montreal|Montreal, Canada]], and the [[University of Calgary]] in [[Calgary, Canada]].

Committed throughout his life both to undergraduate teaching and research, his interests continued to expand throughout his career. His research in [[photochemistry]] contributed to environmental science (particularly soil decontamination, waste treatment, and small-community water systems). In collaboration with his wife, the economic historian Dr. Martha Whitney Langford (b. 1938- d. 2009),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/legacyremembers/martha-langford-obituary?id=45380055|title=Martha Langford Obituary (2009) - Legacy Remembers|website=Legacy.com}}</ref> he pursued research into science policy in Canada, as well as the dynamics of scientific, economic, and entrepreneurial innovation.

He served as associate vice-rector for research at Concordia University, and as vice-president (Research) at the University of Calgary, as well as many roles in federal and provincial research agencies, and scientific organizations, including the [[Arctic Institute of North America]], THECIS (The Center for Innovation Studies).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thecis.ca/dr-cooper-langford-blog-15/|title=Dr. Cooper Langford Blog #15}}</ref> and the Calgary Science Center (later known as [[Telus Spark]]).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sparkscience.ca/|title=TELUS Spark Science Centre|website=www.sparkscience.ca}}</ref> He was granted fellowship of the Royal Society of Canada in 1992. 

Langford was the co-author of two significant introductory chemistry textbooks. The Development of Chemical Principles  (1969, reprinted 1995, with Ralph A. Beebe) was designed to guide undergraduate students through the fundamentals of chemistry by following the history of their development.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Bq8aDsluyggC|title=The Development of Chemical Principles|first1=Cooper Harold|last1=Langford|first2=Ralph Alonzo|last2=Beebe|date=January 1, 1995|publisher=Courier Corporation|isbn=9780486683591 |via=Google Books}}</ref> He also co-wrote the first and second editions of Inorganic Chemistry (1990, with [[Peter Atkins]] and Duard F. Shriver).<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mCsvAQAAIAAJ|title=Inorganic Chemistry|first1=Duward F.|last1=Shriver|first2=Peter William|last2=Atkins|first3=Cooper Harold|last3=Langford|date=June 28, 1994|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-855397-7 |via=Google Books}}</ref>

Cooper died of pancreatic cancer on March 11, 2018, while seeking treatment at the [[Vernon Jubilee Hospital]] in [[Vernon, British Columbia]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/thestar/obituary.aspx?pid=188478547|title=Dr. Cooper H. Langford|via=Legacy.com|work=Toronto Star|date= March 17, 2018}}</ref>
